title: Improper Integrals
overview:
Every definite integral so far had a finite interval and a bounded integrand. An **improper integral** breaks one of those rules: the interval stretches to infinity, as in $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^2}$, or the integrand blows up somewhere, as in $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}}$. Surprisingly, many such integrals still have finite values. A region can be infinitely long yet have finite area, if it gets thin fast enough.

The definition is a limit. For an infinite interval,
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx = \lim_{t \to \infty} \int_a^t f(x)\,dx.$$
You integrate up to a finite stopping point $t$, get an expression in $t$, and then let $t$ grow. If the limit exists as a finite number, the integral **converges** to that number. If the limit is infinite or does not exist, the integral **diverges**. An integral over $(-\infty, \infty)$ is split at any point into two pieces, and both must converge.

For an integrand that is infinite at an endpoint, the same trick applies from the other side. If $f$ blows up at $b$,
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{t \to b^-} \int_a^t f(x)\,dx.$$
If the bad point is in the middle of the interval, split there and treat each side separately. Missing an interior blow-up is the classic trap: $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{dx}{x^2}$ is not $-2$; it diverges, because $\frac{1}{x^2}$ is infinite at $x = 0$.

The benchmark family is $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^p}$, which converges exactly when $p > 1$. So $\frac{1}{x^2}$ gives a finite area but $\frac{1}{x}$ does not, even though both go to zero. Near zero the rule flips: $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{x^p}$ converges exactly when $p < 1$.

When an integral is too hard to evaluate but you only need to know whether it converges, use **comparison**. If $0 \le f(x) \le g(x)$ and $\int g$ converges, then $\int f$ converges too (it is squeezed under a finite area). If $0 \le g(x) \le f(x)$ and $\int g$ diverges, then $\int f$ diverges. The $p$-integrals and $e^{-x}$ are the usual comparison partners.
keyIdeas: Infinite interval: $\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx = \lim_{t \to \infty} \int_a^t f(x)\,dx$. Converges if the limit is finite, diverges otherwise.
Infinite integrand at an endpoint: replace that endpoint by $t$ and take the one-sided limit. For a blow-up inside the interval, split there; both pieces must converge.
$p$-test at infinity: $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^p}$ converges exactly when $p > 1$. Near zero: $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{x^p}$ converges exactly when $p < 1$.
Going to zero is not enough: $\frac{1}{x} \to 0$ but $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x}$ diverges.
Comparison: for $0 \le f \le g$, convergence of $\int g$ forces convergence of $\int f$; divergence of $\int f$ forces divergence of $\int g$.
An integral over $(-\infty, \infty)$ is two improper integrals; never evaluate it as a single symmetric limit.

workedExamples.title: Two tails that look alike
steps: Replace the infinite limit by $t$. First integral: $\int_1^t x^{-2}\,dx = \left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_1^t = -\frac{1}{t} + 1$.
Let $t \to \infty$: $-\frac{1}{t} \to 0$, so the integral converges to $1$. An infinitely long region with area exactly 1.
Let $t \to \infty$: $\ln t \to \infty$. The integral diverges. The region under $\frac{1}{x}$ has infinite area even though the curve goes to zero.
Why the difference: $\frac{1}{x^2}$ shrinks fast enough that the tail areas add up to something finite; $\frac{1}{x}$ shrinks too slowly. The dividing line is exactly $p = 1$.

workedExamples.title: A spike at the endpoint
steps: The integrand is infinite at $x = 0$, so the integral is improper at the lower limit. Replace $0$ by $t$ and take $t \to 0^+$.
Let $t \to 0^+$: $2\sqrt{t} \to 0$, so the integral converges to $2$.
Interpretation: the spike at zero is infinitely tall but so thin that its area is finite. This matches the rule that $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{x^p}$ converges when $p < 1$, and here $p = \frac{1}{2}$.

workedExamples.title: Parts with a limit
steps: Replace $\infty$ by $t$ and find the antiderivative by parts with $u = x$, $dv = e^{-x}\,dx$, so $du = dx$, $v = -e^{-x}$: $\int x e^{-x}\,dx = -x e^{-x} + \int e^{-x}\,dx = -x e^{-x} - e^{-x}$.
Evaluate from $0$ to $t$: $\left[ -x e^{-x} - e^{-x} \right]_0^t = \left( -t e^{-t} - e^{-t} \right) - (0 - 1) = 1 - t e^{-t} - e^{-t}$.
Now the limit. Clearly $e^{-t} \to 0$. For $t e^{-t} = \frac{t}{e^t}$, both top and bottom go to infinity; by l'Hospital's rule the limit is $\lim \frac{1}{e^t} = 0$. Exponentials beat polynomials.
So the integral converges to $1$. This integral is the first of a famous family: $\int_0^\infty x^n e^{-x}\,dx = n!$, and here $n = 1$.

workedExamples.title: Deciding convergence by comparison
steps: There is no elementary antiderivative for $e^{-x^2}$, so a direct limit is impossible. Try comparison with something you can integrate.
For $x \ge 1$, $x^2 \ge x$, so $-x^2 \le -x$ and therefore $e^{-x^2} \le e^{-x}$. The integrand is squeezed below $e^{-x}$ on the whole interval.
The comparison integral converges: $\int_1^\infty e^{-x}\,dx = \lim_{t \to \infty} \left[ -e^{-x} \right]_1^t = \lim_{t \to \infty} \left( e^{-1} - e^{-t} \right) = \frac{1}{e}$.
Since $0 \le e^{-x^2} \le e^{-x}$ and the larger integral is finite, $\int_1^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx$ converges, and its value is at most $\frac{1}{e} \approx 0.368$. (Its actual value is about $0.139$.)

Note what comparison does and does not give: it proves convergence and gives a bound, but not the exact value. For the exact value you need numerical methods or the Gaussian integral from multivariable calculus.

commonMistakes: Ignoring an interior blow-up. $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{dx}{x^2}$ evaluated as $\left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_{-1}^{1} = -2$ is nonsense: the integrand is positive, so the integral cannot be negative. Split at $0$; each piece diverges.
Concluding that an integral converges because the integrand goes to zero. $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x}$ has an integrand that goes to zero and still diverges.

Writing $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^2} = \left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_1^\infty$ and plugging in $\infty$ as if it were a number. Write the limit explicitly; it keeps you honest when the limit does not exist.

Getting the $p$-test backwards near zero. At infinity you need $p > 1$; near zero you need $p < 1$. Check: $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = 2$ converges with $p = \frac{1}{2}$, while $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{x}$ diverges.
Using comparison in the wrong direction. Knowing $f \le g$ and $\int g$ diverges tells you nothing about $\int f$. The bound must be on the useful side.
whyItMatters: Improper integrals are everywhere in science: the total probability under a bell curve is $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}$, escape velocity is an integral to infinity, and the Laplace transform that solves differential equations is $\int_0^\infty$ by definition. They are also the direct link to infinite series: the Integral Test in Chapter 11 says a series converges exactly when the matching improper integral does, so the $p$-test here becomes the $p$-series test there.

checkYourself.q: Does $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^3}$ converge? If so, to what?

checkYourself.a: No. Near zero the test needs $p < 1$, and here $p = 2$. Directly: $\int_t^1 x^{-2}\,dx = \frac{1}{t} - 1 \to \infty$.

checkYourself.q: You want to show $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^2 + 5}$ converges. What do you compare with?

readingGuide: Find the definition of an improper integral over an infinite interval and write in your own words what "convergent" and "divergent" mean.
Locate the $p$-integral result and make sure you can explain why $p = 1$ is the boundary case.
Before reading the example with an integrand that is infinite inside the interval, predict what goes wrong if you integrate straight across.
Find the Comparison Theorem and note the direction of each inequality; then look at how the examples choose a comparison function.
Look for the discussion of $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}$ and why it must be split into two integrals.
